item.title: Benchmarking Quantum Feature Encoding Strategies for Binary Classification with QSVM
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Incorporating pairwise classical feature dependencies into quantum feature maps via controlled-RY(θ) gates affects QSVM binary classification, but simpler encodings (Angle-RY and Z feature Map) often achieve the top composite Quantum Feature Encoding Score by reducing circuit cost and generalization gap.

Grade 0.501 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Machine Learning in Feature Hilbert Spaces” · Murat Kurt

Figure

Training and test classification accuracy across 11 encoding strategies for the EEG Eye State classification dataset.

Asks

How does incorporating statistical dependency structures of classical data into quantum feature maps affect QSVM classification performance and circuit complexity compared to predefined conventional quantum feature maps?

But

Evaluated via state vector simulation on five binary classification datasets, using PCA reduction (14 components) for high-dimensional data, without physical hardware noise.

Tools

Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) · State vector simulation · controlled-R_Y(θ) (CRY) encoding · Pearson, Spearman, Kendall Tau, Mutual Information, Distance Correlation · Z and ZZ feature maps

Abstract

The way in which classical data are encoded into quantum states plays a significant role in both classification performance and quantum circuit complexity in Quantum Machine Learning. In this study, the effects of different quantum feature encoding strategies on Quantum Support Vector Machine performance were investigated using five binary classification datasets. In particular, the statistical relationships between features were incorporated into quantum circuits through \(RY(θ)\) and controlled-\(RY(θ)\) gates, and this approach was compared with conventional quantum feature maps. The results demonstrate that incorporating statistical relationships into the encoding process can influence classification performance. However, more complex and densely entangled circuits do not necessarily yield higher performance. In addition, a composite evaluation metric was employed to jointly assess predictive performance, generalization, and circuit cost. The findings across the five datasets indicate that the choice of quantum feature encoding strategy should account for the underlying structure of the data and that predictive performance should be evaluated together with quantum circuit complexity.

item.title: Quantum SEDONet: Spectrally-Embedded Quantum Deep Operator Networks for Partial Differential Equations
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Spectral coordinate embedding for Quantum DeepONet trunk networks reduces mean relative L2 error across four PDE benchmarks by 36.0% to 54.1%. Qubit count and circuit depth remain completely unchanged.

Grade 0.369 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes” · Muhammad Abid, Arth Sojitra, Bipin Tiwari, Omer San

Figure

Mean relative L2 test error for the advection benchmark. Shows Quantum SEDONet cutting baseline Quantum DeepONet error from 3.463% to 1.744% across 200 test samples.

Asks

Can coordinate-matched classical spectral embeddings eliminate spectral bias in Quantum DeepONet trunk networks without increasing quantum resource costs?

Before

Baseline Quantum DeepONet mean relative L2 error was 1.159% (antiderivative), 3.463% (advection), 2.313% (Burgers), and 5.889% (channel Poisson).

But

Ideal, noiseless, infinite-shot quantum simulation only; single training seed per arm; tested exclusively on smooth or strongly smoothed PDE solutions.

Tools

Quantum DeepONet · unary amplitude encoding · reconfigurable beam-splitter (RBS) gates · Chebyshev expansion · Fourier feature embedding

Abstract

Quantum DeepONet accelerates neural-operator inference by evaluating an orthogonally parameterized network on a quantum computer, reproducing in ideal simulation the accuracy of its classical counterpart at asymptotically lower inference cost. Its trunk network, however, receives query coordinates with limited spectral structure, requiring the network to learn oscillatory features through its nonlinearities. We propose Quantum SEDONet (Spectral-Embedded Deep Operator Network), which assigns each trunk coordinate a spectral basis according to its boundary condition: Fourier features for periodic coordinates and Chebyshev features for bounded, non-periodic coordinates. The basis is selected per coordinate rather than per problem, allowing both representations within a single problem. Under unary amplitude encoding, the embedding incurs no additional qubits or circuit depth when its dimension remains within the network width, while increasing the parameter count by only a few percent. Across four benchmarks, Quantum SEDONet reduces the mean relative L2 error by 54.1% for the antiderivative, 49.6% for advection, 36.0% for Burgers, and 36.2% for a mixed-boundary channel Poisson problem. Quantum and classical evaluation paths agree to within 10^-8 throughout. The channel Poisson problem simultaneously uses Fourier features in the periodic direction and Chebyshev features in the bounded direction, demonstrating coordinate-wise boundary-matched spectral embedding without additional quantum-resource cost.

item.title: Quantum Resource Estimation for Simulating the SYK Model with Trotterization, qDRIFT, and Asymmetric Qubitization
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Asymmetric qubitization outperforms Trotterization and qDRIFT in T-gate scaling for SYK simulation, requiring under 5×108 T gates for N=100 Majorana modes at total error εtotal=10−4 (versus >4×109 for qDRIFT), despite needing 159 qubits instead of 50.

Grade 0.365 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum machine learning” · Brian Goldsmith, Larissa Kroell, Nishna Aerabati

Figure

Qubit count (top) and total T gates at εtotal=10−4 (bottom) versus number of Majorana modes N for Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization at t=1. Asymmetric qubitization requires more qubits (159 vs 50 at N=100) but yields orders of magnitude fewer T gates.

Asks

What are the concrete qubit and T-gate resource requirements for simulating the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model across Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization algorithms?

But

Theoretical worst-case upper bounds used for PPR method resource scaling; assumed evolution time t=1 and split error equally between algorithm and rotation synthesis (εalg=εrot).

Tools

PsiQuantum Construct (Workbench framework) · Asymmetric qubitization with Quantum Signal Processing · Second-order Trotter-Suzuki decomposition · qDRIFT randomized compilation · Jordan-Wigner transformation

Abstract

The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model has been identified as a promising candidate to run on early fault-tolerant quantum computers due to the relatively modest resources required to probe non-trivial physics (namely holographic duality and AdS/CFT correspondence). As such, it is crucial that the details of how to run such a simulation are well understood. Using PsiQuantum's Construct platform, we implement and analyze three different approaches to simulate the SYK model: Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization with Quantum Signal Processing. We provide an open-source library containing implementations for SYK simulation using all three methods, which we use to obtain quantum resource estimates for qubit and T gate count as functions of the number of Majorana modes and precision. We find that while qDRIFT and Trotterization benefit from a lower qubit count, the large number of T gates required lead to asymmetric qubitization being advantageous in most cases. This reinforces previous theoretical considerations. We intend both the implementations and the estimates to be useful for researchers to continue to study the SYK model and understand how the techniques and resources vary.
